screens.title: Arrays & Vectors: The Foundations of Game Collections
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll build an intuitive understanding of two essential linear data structures in C++: fixed-size C-style arrays and dynamic std::vector. You will learn why contiguous memory matters for cache speed, what constant-time index access means in practice, and why vectors are the common choice for most game collections. We’ll walk through a simple inventory and an active-enemy list as concrete examples, show how out-of-bounds access can corrupt memory, and demonstrate how reallocation works when a vector grows. You’ll also see practical mitigations, like reserve(), and a common removal pattern used in games to avoid costly element shifts. By the end you should be able to choose between a C-array and a vector for typical game tasks, know how to avoid the most common mistakes, and apply simple optimizations to keep frame rates stable. Consider a particle system or projectile list in your next prototype and ask where reserve() could prevent a frame hitch.

screens.title: C-style Arrays — Memory Layout and Indexing
screens.narratorSegment: A C-style array is a contiguous block of memory with elements of a single type laid out one after another. This layout means the address of element at index i is the base address plus i times the element size. In games that need predictable memory and minimal allocation overhead — for example, a fixed-size tile grid or a small lookup table known at compile time — a C-array can be a good fit. A concrete example: an array of five integer player scores uses exactly five consecutive integer slots; the program can compute the address of the fifth element without iterating. A common misconception is that raw arrays are always faster than vectors; while access speed is equal because both are contiguous, arrays lack built-in safety and resizing convenience. The biggest hazard is out-of-bounds access: reading or writing index 5 in a size-5 array leads to undefined behavior. To practice, write a small array, index all valid positions, and deliberately try an out-of-bounds read in a controlled debug build to see how it fails. Key takeaway: use C-style arrays when size is fixed and predictable, but be disciplined about bounds and lifetime.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: C-style arrays provide contiguous, fixed-size storage and O(1) index access but lack resizing and safety mechanisms.

content.html:
Core Concept
C-style Arrays — Memory Layout
Elements are laid out contiguously. Address = base + index * element_size. Fast direct access, fixed size, no automatic resizing.
Bullets
  • Contiguous memory improves cache locality and iteration speed.
  • Index arithmetic allows O(1) random access to any element.
  • Cannot change size at runtime without manual allocation and copy.
Common mistake
Out-of-bounds access leads to undefined behavior and corrupted data.
Key Takeaway

Use C-style arrays for fixed-size, performance-critical storage, but always check indices and lifetimes.

// Example of a C-style array
int playerScores[5]; // An array to hold 5 integer scores
playerScores[0] = 100;
playerScores[1] = 150;
// ...
// Common mistake: Out-of-bounds access
// playerScores[5] = 200; // This is an error! Valid indices are 0-4.

  // Process playerScores[i]

screens.title: std::vector Basics — Push, Access, Iterate
screens.narratorSegment: std::vector provides the convenience of a dynamically sized array while preserving contiguous storage and O(1) index access. You create an empty vector and push elements onto it; its size() reports how many elements are stored, and capacity() shows how many it can hold before reallocating. Use operator[] for fast access when you’re certain an index is valid; use at() when you want bounds-checked access that throws on error, which is helpful during debugging. In practice, vectors are the go-to container for game entity lists and inventories because they are simple to iterate and interoperate with standard algorithms. As a concrete example, imagine an inventory of three strings used to display items in a UI. You push back three items, check size and capacity, and then iterate to render names. A common misconception is that vectors always copy on push; they only copy when capacity is exceeded and reallocation happens. When using vectors in tight loops, monitor capacity changes and apply reserve() when you can predict a high-water mark. For safety practice, alternate operator[] and at() to see behavior in debug builds, and always consider reserve() for performance-sensitive lists.

keyIdea.title: Vector basics
keyIdea.text: Vectors combine contiguous storage with dynamic growth; operator[] is fast, at() is safer, and reserve() controls reallocations.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
std::vector Basics
Dynamic array with size, capacity, push_back, operator[] and at(). Use reserve() to avoid reallocations.
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
  std::vector<std::string> inventory; // dynamic array

  // Add items
  inventory.push_back("Health Potion");
  inventory.push_back("Iron Sword");
  inventory.push_back("Wooden Shield");

  std::cout << "Size: " << inventory.size() << std::endl;
  std::cout << "Capacity: " << inventory.capacity() << std::endl;

  // Access
  std::cout << "First: " << inventory[0] << std::endl;
  std::cout << "Last: " << inventory.back() << std::endl;

  // Iterate
  for (const auto &item : inventory) {
    std::cout << "- " << item << std::endl;
  }
}
Explanation cards
Size vs Capacity
size() is the number of stored elements; capacity() is how many can fit before reallocation.
Operator[] vs at()
operator[] is unchecked and fast; at() throws on invalid indices and aids debugging.
Common pattern
Use reserve() for predictable maximums and prefer vectors for entity lists you iterate every frame.
Key Takeaway

Vectors give you array performance with dynamic sizing; manage capacity when performance matters.

screens.title: Vector Reallocation — How Growth Works
screens.narratorSegment: When a std::vector runs out of reserved capacity and you push another element, it reallocates: the vector allocates a new block of memory, copies or moves all existing elements into the new block, deallocates the old block, and then inserts the new element. Many implementations grow capacity geometrically, often doubling, to amortize copies over many insertions. The visible effect is that most push operations are cheap, but occasional pushes cost O(n) to copy n elements. In a game loop where you add objects frequently — for instance, spawning many projectiles in a few frames — these occasional O(n) operations can cause frame hitches. A concrete mitigation is reserve(): if you call reserve(N) before adding elements, the vector will allocate enough space for N elements and avoid reallocations until you exceed that amount. Another practical pattern is pre-sizing with resize() if you need default-constructed elements immediately. Misconception: doubling means reallocation will never cost you; it reduces frequency but does not eliminate the occasional copy. Key takeaway: profile capacity changes and use reserve() when you can predict a peak. Vector Reallocation — How Growth Works means reallocation moves elements to a new block when capacity is exceeded; reserve() prevents frequent reallocations and reduces runtime hitches.. In practical terms, what happens when capacity is exceeded and why it costs time. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Reallocation
keyIdea.text: Reallocation moves elements to a new block when capacity is exceeded; reserve() prevents frequent reallocations and reduces runtime hitches.

content.html:
Process Flow
Vector Reallocation Steps
1. Need more space
2. Allocate larger block
3. Copy/move elements
4. Free old block
Each reallocation is O(n) due to copying elements. Doubling capacity reduces frequency, making amortized push_back cost O(1), but individual reallocations still spike cost in a given frame.
// Pre-allocating to avoid reallocation
std::vector<int> particleIDs;
particleIDs.reserve(1000); // no reallocations up to 1000 pushes
for (int i = 0; i < 500; ++i) {
  particleIDs.push_back(i);
}
Why it matters for games
  • Reallocations cause brief CPU and memory pressure.
  • Frequent reallocations can create visible frame drops.
  • reserve() is a simple, effective optimization when peak size is predictable.
Misconception
Doubling capacity removes reallocations forever — not true. It only reduces their frequency; they still occur when capacity is exceeded.
Key Takeaway

Predict peak sizes and call reserve() to keep push_back operations smooth during gameplay.

screens.title: Removing Elements — erase vs pop_back vs swap-and-pop
screens.narratorSegment: Removing elements from a std::vector has different costs depending on where you delete. pop_back() removes the last element in O(1) time. Erasing an element in the middle requires shifting all later elements down, which is O(n) in the number of shifted elements. In games where ordering does not matter — for example, many projectile systems — a common optimization is swap-and-pop: swap the element-to-remove with the last element, then pop_back(). This achieves an effective O(1) removal but changes order. Use swap-and-pop when element order is not significant. Another pattern is using remove_if followed by erase to batch-remove defeated enemies at the end of a frame; this reduces repeated shifting during the frame and consolidates cost. A misconception is that erase is cheap for small vectors; while smaller n means smaller cost, many small erases per frame add up. Consider design: if you frequently remove arbitrary items and must keep order, a different structure may be required. Practice both patterns and observe timing to choose the best approach for your game’s needs. In practical terms, performance trade-offs when deleting elements from a vector. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Removal trade-offs
keyIdea.text: pop_back is O(1); erase in middle shifts elements O(n); swap-and-pop gives O(1) removal when order isn’t required.

content.html:
Comparison
Erase patterns and costs
pop_back()
Removes last element in O(1). Best for stack-like usage.
erase(iterator)
Shifts subsequent elements, O(n) cost proportional to elements moved.
swap-and-pop
Swap target with last element, pop_back(); O(1) but order-changing.
Concrete example
// Swap-and-pop removal
std::vector<Enemy> active;
int removeIndex = 2; // enemy defeated
active[removeIndex] = std::move(active.back());
active.pop_back(); // fast O(1) removal if order doesn't matter
Tip: If you must keep order and frequently remove middle elements, measure performance. Batch removals with remove_if + erase once per frame often performs better than many erases during updates.
Pro Tip

When order is irrelevant, prefer swap-and-pop to keep removals cheap every frame.

screens.title: Entity Lists in Games — Inventory, Enemies, and Particles
screens.narratorSegment: Many game systems rely on fast iteration over large lists: inventories, active enemies, particles, and projectiles. std::vector is typically the workhorse for these lists because it provides contiguous storage for efficient iteration and cache-friendly access patterns during physics, AI updates, and rendering. For inventories where the number of slots is fixed and known at compile time, a C-style array or fixed-size container is appropriate. For particles or enemies whose counts vary during gameplay, vector’s dynamic sizing and iteration convenience usually win. When structuring an entity manager using vector, reserve an estimated maximum to avoid reallocations, store simple structs or indices to minimize copying, and prefer swap-and-pop removals if you can tolerate unordered lists. Also, consider that erase operations that maintain order are expensive; design systems to batch removals at frame boundaries. A realistic example: reserve for a maximum of 100 enemies, push_back on spawn, swap-and-pop to remove defeated enemies during update, and iterate through the vector to update positions and render. The core design decision is predictable performance versus strict ordering. In practical terms, how vectors power common game systems and where arrays still fit. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: System design
keyIdea.text: Use vectors for dynamic entity lists and arrays for fixed-size storage; design removal patterns around ordering needs to maintain performance.

content.html:
Architecture
Entity list patterns
Design vectors to hold compact entity data, reserve expected peaks, and choose removal patterns based on order needs.
Common uses
  • Particle systems — vector with reserve for peak particles.
  • Projectile lists — swap-and-pop acceptable if order is irrelevant.
  • Inventory — fixed-size arrays or vectors sized to slot count.
Key Takeaway

Match container choice to dynamics: arrays for fixed slots, vectors for changing lists, and reserve to stabilize performance.

Entity manager sketch
struct Enemy { int id; int health; };

std::vector<Enemy> activeEnemies;
activeEnemies.reserve(100); // anticipate peak

// spawn
activeEnemies.push_back({1, 50});

// remove using swap-and-pop
int i = 2;
activeEnemies[i] = std::move(activeEnemies.back());
activeEnemies.pop_back();

// update loop
for (auto &e : activeEnemies) {
  // update position, health, render
}
Practice: implement spawn, damage, remove, and render loops. Measure frame time with and without reserve() to see reallocations' impact.

Create a vector of Enemy, call reserve() for an anticipated maximum, then push_back new enemies when they spawn. When an enemy is defeated, mark it or remove it using swap-and-pop or remove_if plus erase at the end of the frame. The provided template includes reserve(100) and demonstrates taking damage, using remove_if to prune defeated enemies, and iterating to print remaining enemies. A common issue is modifying a vector while iterating using iterators; one safe approach is to mark elements and then do a single remove_if+erase pass. Another is to collect indices for removal and then handle them after the update loop. Practice both and observe which fits your gameplay loop. The final step is to print size and capacity after operations to confirm reserve prevented reallocations. This template is deliberately minimal so you can extend it with positions, velocities, and render flags as you build your game prototype. content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Enemy Manager Starter
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>

struct Enemy { int id; int health; std::string name; };

int main() {
  std::vector<Enemy> activeEnemies;
  activeEnemies.reserve(100); // pre-allocate for peak

  // Add enemies
  activeEnemies.push_back({1, 50, "Goblin"});
  activeEnemies.push_back({2, 75, "Orc"});

  // Simulate damage
  activeEnemies[0].health -= 60; // Goblin defeated

  // Remove defeated enemies using remove_if + erase
  activeEnemies.erase(std::remove_if(activeEnemies.begin(), activeEnemies.end(),
                                     [](const Enemy &e){ return e.health <= 0; }),
                      activeEnemies.end());

  // Print remaining
  for (const auto &e : activeEnemies) {
    std::cout << e.name << " (ID: " << e.id << ") Health: " << e.health << std::endl;
  }
}
Explanation & Tips
  • reserve(100) prevents reallocations up to 100 inserts.
  • remove_if + erase batches deletions and reduces per-frame shifting.
  • swap-and-pop is faster but changes order; use when order isn't required.
Key Takeaway

Start with a reserve and simple removal pattern, then profile and tune based on your game’s behavior.

screens.title: Capacity vs Size — Important Distinction
screens.narratorSegment: size() and capacity() describe different aspects of a vector. size() is how many elements are currently stored and iterated over. capacity() is how many elements the vector can hold without reallocating. Capacity is an implementation-visible buffer and can be larger than size. This matters because push_back increments size, but if size surpasses capacity, reallocation occurs and elements are copied or moved. A frequent debugging technique is to print capacity before and after batches of insertions to detect unexpected reallocations. Reserving capacity sets the capacity directly, preventing growth-related reallocations until the reserved amount is exceeded. Another practical method is resize() to create a vector with default-initialized elements immediately, which sets size and may also adjust capacity. Misconceptions include expecting capacity to shrink automatically after many erases; shrink_to_fit can request a reduction but does not guarantee immediate behavior. In game loops, controlling capacity avoids unpredictable allocations and keeps frame time stable. Practice reading capacity() in test builds while running mass spawns to spot reallocations. Definition
Capacity vs Size
Understanding this difference helps you predict when reallocations will occur and how to prevent them using reserve().
std::vector<int> v;

screens.title: When to Use Arrays vs Vectors
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between a C-style array and std::vector comes down to predictability, safety, and convenience. Use a C-style array when the number of elements is a compile-time constant, lifetime is simple, and you need minimal overhead. Use std::vector when you need dynamic sizing, automatic lifetime management, and standard library interoperability. For game examples: use an array for a fixed-size inventory UI that never grows beyond defined slots; use a vector for an enemy list that spawns and despawns frequently. Other considerations: if you interact with C APIs that expect raw pointers, arrays or vector. data() both work — vector. data() gives you a pointer while keeping ownership in C++ code. A common misconception is that vectors always allocate; an empty vector may have zero capacity until you reserve. Also, arrays do not provide size metadata at runtime, so tracking size separately is necessary. Use this checklist: is size fixed at compile time? Use array. Do you need growth and algorithm support? Use vector. Do you need predictable real-time behavior? Use reserve and test under load. screens.title: Optimizations & Common Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: This slide collects practical optimizations and pitfalls drawn from the previous examples. First, reserve() early when you know a likely maximum to eliminate reallocation spikes. Second, prefer pop_back or swap-and-pop to keep removals cheap when order does not matter. Third, batch removals with remove_if + erase at frame boundaries rather than erasing repeatedly while iterating. Fourth, use at() in debug builds to catch out-of-bounds errors during development, then switch to operator[] for hot inner loops when you are confident. Fifth, avoid storing large heavy objects directly in vectors; prefer lightweight structs or use move semantics to minimize copy cost during reallocation. A common pitfall is repeatedly calling clear() followed by many push_back operations without reserve, which can cause repeated allocations. Always measure: profiling capacity and frame time while stressing spawns will reveal whether your reserve sizes are sufficient. The practical habit is to test each system under load and iterate on reserve sizes until frame-time is acceptable. Hands-on Practice
Particle System Template
struct Particle { float x,y; float vx,vy; float life; };

std::vector<Particle> particles;
particles.reserve(1000); // try with and without this line

// Burst spawn
for (int i = 0; i < 500; ++i) {
  particles.push_back({0,0, randv(), randv(), 1.0f});
}

// Update and remove dead
for (auto &p : particles) {
  // integrate position
  p.life -= 0.016f;
}
particles.erase(std::remove_if(particles.begin(), particles.end(),
                               [](const Particle &p){ return p.life <= 0.0f; }),
                particles.end());
Experiment checklist
  1. Run with reserve(1000) and measure capacity() changes and frame time.
  2. Run without reserve and compare reallocation frequency and spikes.
  3. Try swap-and-pop removal and note effects on order and performance.

Small code changes like reserve() can have measurable runtime effects. Test under realistic bursts to choose safe defaults.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll build an intuitive understanding of two essential linear data structures in C++: fixed-size C-style arrays and dynamic std::vector. You will learn why contiguous memory matters for cache speed, what constant-time index access means in practice, and why vectors are the common choice for most game collections. We’ll walk through a simple inventory and an active-enemy list as concrete examples, show how out-of-bounds access can corrupt memory, and demonstrate how reallocation works when a vector grows. You’ll also see practical mitigations, like reserve(), and a common removal pattern used in games to avoid costly element shifts. By the end you should be able to choose between a C-array and a vector for typical game tasks, know how to avoid the most common mistakes, and apply simple optimizations to keep frame rates stable. Consider a particle system or projectile list in your next prototype and ask where reserve() could prevent a frame hitch.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the memory layout of a C-style array and why contiguous storage gives fast, constant-time access. You'll describe how std::vector manages capacity and when a reallocation occurs, including the cost of copying elements during that process. You'll identify concrete game scenarios — for example, inventories, particle systems, and active enemy lists — and choose the best data structure for each. Finally, you will implement basic operations: adding elements, accessing elements safely, iterating across collections, and applying reserve() to prevent frequent reallocations. Each objective ties directly to an applied example so you can test the idea immediately in a small game prototype. As you practice, pay attention to the trade-offs between raw arrays and vectors: fixed memory predictability versus flexible growth, and how that affects frame-time stability in gameplay. Consider which objective you’ll try first in your game prototype.

This second objectives slide focuses on safe usage and practical patterns you will practice. You will learn to avoid out-of-bounds access by preferring bounds-checked methods when debugging, to detect reallocation-related hitches by monitoring capacity changes, and to decide when mid-vector erases are acceptable or when swap-and-pop is preferable. You will also practice an entity-manager pattern using std::vector with reserve() and learn the remove_if then erase idiom for bulk deletions at the end of a frame. Each of these skills reduces common runtime problems: corrupted data, frame-rate spikes, and slow removal loops. Practice these skills in small prototypes: start with a 100-particle system where you pre-reserve capacity, then test adding and removing many elements and observe capacity behavior. This focused practice will make these optimizations second nature during level design and runtime tuning.

A C-style array is a contiguous block of memory with elements of a single type laid out one after another. This layout means the address of element at index i is the base address plus i times the element size. In games that need predictable memory and minimal allocation overhead — for example, a fixed-size tile grid or a small lookup table known at compile time — a C-array can be a good fit. A concrete example: an array of five integer player scores uses exactly five consecutive integer slots; the program can compute the address of the fifth element without iterating. A common misconception is that raw arrays are always faster than vectors; while access speed is equal because both are contiguous, arrays lack built-in safety and resizing convenience. The biggest hazard is out-of-bounds access: reading or writing index 5 in a size-5 array leads to undefined behavior. To practice, write a small array, index all valid positions, and deliberately try an out-of-bounds read in a controlled debug build to see how it fails. Key takeaway: use C-style arrays when size is fixed and predictable, but be disciplined about bounds and lifetime.

std::vector provides the convenience of a dynamically sized array while preserving contiguous storage and O(1) index access. You create an empty vector and push elements onto it; its size() reports how many elements are stored, and capacity() shows how many it can hold before reallocating. Use operator[] for fast access when you’re certain an index is valid; use at() when you want bounds-checked access that throws on error, which is helpful during debugging. In practice, vectors are the go-to container for game entity lists and inventories because they are simple to iterate and interoperate with standard algorithms. As a concrete example, imagine an inventory of three strings used to display items in a UI. You push back three items, check size and capacity, and then iterate to render names. A common misconception is that vectors always copy on push; they only copy when capacity is exceeded and reallocation happens. When using vectors in tight loops, monitor capacity changes and apply reserve() when you can predict a high-water mark. For safety practice, alternate operator[] and at() to see behavior in debug builds, and always consider reserve() for performance-sensitive lists.

When a std::vector runs out of reserved capacity and you push another element, it reallocates: the vector allocates a new block of memory, copies or moves all existing elements into the new block, deallocates the old block, and then inserts the new element. Many implementations grow capacity geometrically, often doubling, to amortize copies over many insertions. The visible effect is that most push operations are cheap, but occasional pushes cost O(n) to copy n elements. In a game loop where you add objects frequently — for instance, spawning many projectiles in a few frames — these occasional O(n) operations can cause frame hitches. A concrete mitigation is reserve(): if you call reserve(N) before adding elements, the vector will allocate enough space for N elements and avoid reallocations until you exceed that amount. Another practical pattern is pre-sizing with resize() if you need default-constructed elements immediately. Misconception: doubling means reallocation will never cost you; it reduces frequency but does not eliminate the occasional copy. Key takeaway: profile capacity changes and use reserve() when you can predict a peak. Vector Reallocation — How Growth Works means reallocation moves elements to a new block when capacity is exceeded; reserve() prevents frequent reallocations and reduces runtime hitches.. In practical terms, what happens when capacity is exceeded and why it costs time. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Removing elements from a std::vector has different costs depending on where you delete. pop_back() removes the last element in O(1) time. Erasing an element in the middle requires shifting all later elements down, which is O(n) in the number of shifted elements. In games where ordering does not matter — for example, many projectile systems — a common optimization is swap-and-pop: swap the element-to-remove with the last element, then pop_back(). This achieves an effective O(1) removal but changes order. Use swap-and-pop when element order is not significant. Another pattern is using remove_if followed by erase to batch-remove defeated enemies at the end of a frame; this reduces repeated shifting during the frame and consolidates cost. A misconception is that erase is cheap for small vectors; while smaller n means smaller cost, many small erases per frame add up. Consider design: if you frequently remove arbitrary items and must keep order, a different structure may be required. Practice both patterns and observe timing to choose the best approach for your game’s needs. Removing Elements — erase vs pop_back vs swap-and-pop means pop_back is o(1); erase in middle shifts elements o(n); swap-and-pop gives o(1) removal when order isn’t required.. In practical terms, performance trade-offs when deleting elements from a vector. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Many game systems rely on fast iteration over large lists: inventories, active enemies, particles, and projectiles. std::vector is typically the workhorse for these lists because it provides contiguous storage for efficient iteration and cache-friendly access patterns during physics, AI updates, and rendering. For inventories where the number of slots is fixed and known at compile time, a C-style array or fixed-size container is appropriate. For particles or enemies whose counts vary during gameplay, vector’s dynamic sizing and iteration convenience usually win. When structuring an entity manager using vector, reserve an estimated maximum to avoid reallocations, store simple structs or indices to minimize copying, and prefer swap-and-pop removals if you can tolerate unordered lists. Also, consider that erase operations that maintain order are expensive; design systems to batch removals at frame boundaries. A realistic example: reserve for a maximum of 100 enemies, push_back on spawn, swap-and-pop to remove defeated enemies during update, and iterate through the vector to update positions and render. The core design decision is predictable performance versus strict ordering. size() and capacity() describe different aspects of a vector. size() is how many elements are currently stored and iterated over. capacity() is how many elements the vector can hold without reallocating. Capacity is an implementation-visible buffer and can be larger than size. This matters because push_back increments size, but if size surpasses capacity, reallocation occurs and elements are copied or moved. A frequent debugging technique is to print capacity before and after batches of insertions to detect unexpected reallocations. Reserving capacity sets the capacity directly, preventing growth-related reallocations until the reserved amount is exceeded. Another practical method is resize() to create a vector with default-initialized elements immediately, which sets size and may also adjust capacity. Misconceptions include expecting capacity to shrink automatically after many erases; shrink_to_fit can request a reduction but does not guarantee immediate behavior. In game loops, controlling capacity avoids unpredictable allocations and keeps frame time stable. Practice reading capacity() in test builds while running mass spawns to spot reallocations. Choosing between a C-style array and std::vector comes down to predictability, safety, and convenience. Use a C-style array when the number of elements is a compile-time constant, lifetime is simple, and you need minimal overhead. Use std::vector when you need dynamic sizing, automatic lifetime management, and standard library interoperability. For game examples: use an array for a fixed-size inventory UI that never grows beyond defined slots; use a vector for an enemy list that spawns and despawns frequently. Other considerations: if you interact with C APIs that expect raw pointers, arrays or vector. data() both work — vector. data() gives you a pointer while keeping ownership in C++ code. A common misconception is that vectors always allocate; an empty vector may have zero capacity until you reserve. Also, arrays do not provide size metadata at runtime, so tracking size separately is necessary. Use this checklist: is size fixed at compile time? Use array. Do you need growth and algorithm support? Use vector. Do you need predictable real-time behavior? Use reserve and test under load. This slide collects practical optimizations and pitfalls drawn from the previous examples. First, reserve() early when you know a likely maximum to eliminate reallocation spikes. Second, prefer pop_back or swap-and-pop to keep removals cheap when order does not matter. Third, batch removals with remove_if + erase at frame boundaries rather than erasing repeatedly while iterating. Fourth, use at() in debug builds to catch out-of-bounds errors during development, then switch to operator[] for hot inner loops when you are confident. Fifth, avoid storing large heavy objects directly in vectors; prefer lightweight structs or use move semantics to minimize copy cost during reallocation. A common pitfall is repeatedly calling clear() followed by many push_back operations without reserve, which can cause repeated allocations. Always measure: profiling capacity and frame time while stressing spawns will reveal whether your reserve sizes are sufficient. The practical habit is to test each system under load and iterate on reserve sizes until frame-time is acceptable. Keep these concise concepts in mind as you build game systems. First, C-style arrays are fixed-size and contiguous, offering predictable memory layout and fast index access but no resizing features. Second, std::vector provides dynamic resizing with contiguous storage and keeps O(1) random access; it manages memory for you but can reallocate when capacity is exceeded. Third, contiguous memory improves cache performance and makes iteration fast, which is crucial for per-frame updates. Understanding size, capacity, and reallocation behavior allows you to design systems that avoid unpredictable frame-cost spikes. Keep these three quick reminders handy as you code. First, contiguous memory matters: iteration and random access are fast because elements sit next to each other in memory. Second, std::vector adds convenient dynamic growth but can reallocate and copy elements; reserve() prevents reallocations when you can predict a high-water mark. Third, deletions have costs: pop_back is cheap, erase in the middle shifts elements, and swap-and-pop can give you O(1) removals if ordering is not required.
